The literal meaning of bake-neko is changed cat.
The idea of monstrous cats was especially popular in the Edo period.
In a Sado Island legend, an old woman becomes a bakeneko and flies to Mount Yahiko.
The legend’s link to Myōtara-ten is not an official Hōkōin temple tradition.
Bakeneko belong to Japanese supernatural lore.
Cats seen standing and licking lantern oil may have inspired fear in the Edo period.
The legend tells of an old woman on Sado Island who loved cats.
In the legend people later worshiped the old woman as Myōtara-ten.

baku-mythology.depicted_variant: Baku in the Sankai Ibutsu anatomical variant: one stocky four-legged dream beast whose head has an ELEPHANT TRUNK and TWO ELEPHANT TUSKS but small rounded RHINOCEROS EARS. A stocky BEAR-like grey body, TIGER-like clawed paws, and a CATTLE-like tail, Japanese forest setting. No ordinary tapir head without tusks, no wings.

basis_claims.statement: The term baku denotes both the dream-eating creature and the Malayan tapir.
Baku were known in Japan by the Muromachi period.
The Sankai Ibutsu manuscript describes an elephant's trunk and tusks with rhinoceros ears.
Lafcadio Hearn wrote about a nightmare-eating baku in 1902.

bakunawa.depicted_variant: Bakunawa, the Philippine moon-eating serpentine dragon: one vast curved scaled serpent body, a clearly looped tail and exactly ONE horn on the nose. Its open dragon-like mouth reaches toward the moon above Philippine coastal water. No wings, no human body, no duplicate nose horns.

basis_claims.statement: The bakunawa, the Philippine moon-eating dragon, is a dragon-like serpent of Philippine mythology causing natural phenomena, mainly eclipses; its movements were a geomantic calendar and part of babaylan rituals; it has a looped tail and one nose horn and lives in the sky or underworld.
Through trade with South Asia and Indianization, the bakunawa was syncretized with the Nāga, Rahu and Ketu of Hindu-Buddhist mythology.
Bakunawa is thought to be a compound meaning 'bent snake', from Proto-Western-Malayo-Polynesian *ba(ŋ)kuq ('bent') and *sawa ('large snake'); variants include Vakonawa, Baconaua, Bakonaua.
The most similar is the Tagalog Laho (from Rahu), a serpent-like dragon causing lunar eclipses.
Pre-colonial Cebuanos believed the supreme god Bathala made 7 moons; the bakunawa, amazed, rose from the sea and swallowed them, becoming Bathala's mortal enemy.
To stop the moons being devoured, early Filipinos clanged pots and pans outdoors to startle the bakunawa into disgorging them.
According to Jordan Clark, most recent literary versions derive from Damiana Eugenio's retelling, itself imagined from Fernando Buyser's earlier account.
The first documentation of the bakunawa was in 1628 by Fr. Alonso de Mentrida, an Augustinian missionary, in a Hiligaynon dictionary.
The bakunawa was believed to live in the sky or the underworld.

basan-legendary-bird.depicted_variant: Basan, one enormous CHICKEN-like Japanese bird with rooster head, beak, comb, two bird legs and feathered wings. A glowing flame-like BREATH issues from its beak; its actual feathers are not burning. Mountain bamboo setting. No phoenix body, no serpent tail.

basis_claims.statement: Basan is a bird from Japanese myth and illustrated monster books.
Its body is likened to a large chicken.
Pictures give it a red comb and plumage resembling flames.
Its breath looks like fire, a feature distinct from its feathers.

bashe.depicted_variant: Bashe, one enormous PYTHON-like Chinese serpent, with one broad python head and a continuous thick coiled python body, in a lush river valley beside large trees that show its scale. No elephant being eaten, no legs, no wings, no horns.

basis_claims.statement: Bashe is a python-like giant serpent in Chinese mythology that eats elephants.
Its name combines elements for an elephant-eating snake and a serpent.
Bashe has also been used as an alternative name for pythons.
Early Bashe references occur in the Chu Ci and Shanhaijing.

basilisco-chilote.depicted_variant: Basilisco Chilote: one continuous scaled SERPENT BODY with a reptilian head bearing a clearly visible ROOSTER CREST/comb. Chilean rural woodland at night. No legs, no bat wings, no separate rooster body; show the snake-bodied variant.

basis_claims.statement: The Basilisco chilote originates from Chilota mythology in the southern region of Chile.
The creature has the crest of a rooster and a serpent body.
It feeds on saliva and phlegm, causing victims to dehydrate and perish.

beast-of-bray-road.depicted_variant: Beast of Bray Road in the reported upright variant: a roughly two-metre wolf-headed being with a HUMANLIKE fur-covered torso, two long arms, two upright legs, and large glowing orange-red eyes. Rural Wisconsin roadside at dusk. No horns or wings.

basis_claims.statement: The Beast of Bray Road is the name given to a wolf-like creature reportedly seen in or near Elkhorn, Walworth County, Wisconsin.
Named after the farm road where it was first supposedly seen, reports in the 1980s and 1990s led the local paper Walworth County Week to assign reporter Linda Godfrey to the story.
Skeptics hold that it is probably a misidentification of known animals, most likely gray wolves.
Witnesses often describe it as 1.8–2.1 m tall, humanlike in body and furred, with a wolf's head and large glowing red or orange eyes.
It is said to move on four legs and on two, and some reports liken it more to a traditional werewolf or Bigfoot.
It was supposedly first seen on two nights running in 1936 on the grounds of St. Coletta School in Jefferson, where a night watchman saw it digging at an Indian burial mound.
One witness claimed that after hitting something on Bray Road and getting out to look, a large red-eyed wolf-like creature chased her back to the car, leaving claw marks on the rear door.
Others suggest it may be an American black bear with mange.
According to the French article, the name has since been applied to any sighting of an unknown creature from southern Wisconsin to northern Illinois.
According to the Spanish article, it is a supposed pseudo-cryptid whose first reported sighting dates only to the 1980s.

beast-of-busco.depicted_variant: Beast of Busco: one exceptionally HUGE SNAPPING TURTLE with a heavy ridged turtle shell, broad beaked snapping-turtle head, four stout reptilian legs and a long reptilian tail, emerging from an Indiana freshwater pond. No dragon head or tentacles.

basis_claims.statement: The Beast of Busco is a legendary Indiana creature described as an unusually large snapping turtle.
Residents reported it near Churubusco, Indiana, in 1949, prompting a month-long search with national attention.
Despite great efforts, no conclusive evidence was found.

bessie-lake-monster.depicted_variant: Bessie of Lake Erie, one very long GREY snake-like lake creature, with one plain serpent head and a continuous smooth serpentine body, partly surfaced in misty lake water. No horns, flippers, legs or wings; no plesiosaur anatomy.

basis_claims.statement: In northeastern Ohio and Michigan folklore, Bessie is a Lake Erie monster, also called South Bay Bessie or The Lake Erie Monster.
The first recorded sighting was in 1817.
Bessie is reported as snake-like, 30 to 40 ft long and greyish.

bifang.depicted_variant: Bifang as described in the Shanhaijing: a crane-like bird with exactly ONE leg, GREEN plumage with clear RED markings and a WHITE beak. Standing with the single leg completely visible beside a Chinese woodland stream. No second leg hidden behind, no flames.

basis_claims.statement: Bifang is a Chinese mythological bird often portrayed with one leg.
The Hanfeizi describes it as an auspicious bird accompanying the Yellow Emperor.
The Shanhaijing gives crane-like features, red markings on green, and a white beak.
Bifang is associated with an omen of fire.
The Huainanzi associates this bird with the wood element.

bigfoot.depicted_variant: Bigfoot: one very tall broad ape-like biped, entirely covered in dark-brown hair with a recognizably apelike face, two arms and two feet, walking upright in Pacific Northwest conifer woods. Natural coarse fur, no horns, no claws added, no clothing.

basis_claims.statement: Bigfoot is a large and mysterious humanoid creature purported to inhabit the wild and forested areas of Oregon and the West Coast of North America.
Bigfoot is also known as Sasquatch, an Anglicization of the name Sasq’ets, from the Halq’emeylem language
hair-covered bipeds with apelike features up to eight feet tall that leave correspondingly large footprints.
They are generally characterized as nonaggressive animals, whose shyness and humanlike intelligence make them elusive
Most scientists, however, remain skeptics and dismiss the phenomenon as the product of the mistaken identification of known animals or elaborate hoaxes
stories about Bigfoot have entered into oral tradition and become part of regional folklore.
Local Native Americans used this event to discuss publicly their own knowledge of tsiatko, hirsute “wild Indians” of the woods
After 1958, woods workers east and west of the Cascade Mountains began to report seeing creatures and discovering their immense tracks along logging roads
Sasquatches long populated the mythologies of American Indian tribes in the Pacific Northwest
those 1958 footprints transformed the myth into a media sensation.
The tracks were planted near Bluff Creek in Northern California by a man named Ray Wallace
In 1967, Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed a few seconds of a hairy creature walking on two legs
The hairs are of deer family origin.
this is not evidence that the FBI endorsed the existence of Bigfoot
Naish has written that Bigfoot is the modern American “manifestation of a human-wide cultural concept, not a zoological reality.”

bixi.depicted_variant: Bixi, the Chinese dragon-tortoise: one TURTLE body with a substantial rounded shell, four sturdy turtle legs, a turtle tail and exactly one DRAGON HEAD, carrying an upright old stone stele on its shell. Chinese temple courtyard. No human face, no wings, no extra heads.

basis_claims.statement: Bixi is a Chinese mythological figure portrayed as a dragon with a turtle shell.
He is described as one of the Dragon King's nine sons.
Bixi stone sculptures form decorative supports for commemorative steles and tablets.
A Nanjing Museum funerary jar dated 272 depicts a miniature stele-bearing tortoise.
Ming-era Hongwu regulations restricted tortoise-based stelae according to rank.

boiuna.depicted_variant: Boiuna, the Brazilian Amazon BLACK SNAKE: one massive glossy BLACK serpentine body, one large snake head and a long coiling tail surfacing from a dark Amazon river at night. No wings, legs, hair or dragon antlers.

basis_claims.statement: Boiuna ("Black Snake") is a creature of Brazilian mythology, also called Cobra-Grande ("Large Serpent") and Mboiaçu.
The Boiuna is a nocturnal black snake, the most powerful creature of the Amazon rivers.
It can become a canoe, a sailboat or a woman to frighten fishermen entering its territory.

bozalosc.depicted_variant: Bozalosc in the recorded Sorbian variant: one adult female spirit in a modest WHITE dress, with long unkempt hair and RED eyes, standing near an elder bush by a quiet European village. No horns, wings, fangs or other beings.

basis_claims.statement: Božalość, also transliterated Božaloshtsh or Bozaloshtsh, is a messenger of misfortune or death in Wendish mythology (the Wends, Lusatian Sorbs).
In German ethnographic sources the name was translated as "Gottesklage", that is, "God's Lament".
An 1886 article, Das Spreewaldhaus by W. v. Schulenburg, links it with the elder bush and describes it as a woman in white with long, unkempt hair and red eyes.
Biren Bonnerjea describes it as a little long-haired woman who weeps under the window of someone about to die.
A parallel creature is the bože sedleško, described as a child in white clothes.
The appearance of a bože sedleško signals coming misfortune: death, fire, epidemics, flood and so on.

buggane.depicted_variant: Buggane in the attested natural shaggy form: one enormous coarse BLACK-haired creature with a heavy mane, eyes bright like torches and sharply protruding glittering TUSKS, outside a ruined Manx stone church. Broad beastlike body. No wings, no Balinese mask or flame-covered body.

basis_claims.statement: In Manx folklore a buggane (or boagane) was a huge ogre-like creature native to the Isle of Man, which some consider akin to the Scandinavian troll.
A malevolent shapeshifter, the buggane can appear as a large black calf or a human with a horse's ears or hooves, and is big enough to tear the roof off a church.
Its natural form is 'covered with a mane of coarse, black hair; it had eyes like torches, and glittering sharp tusks'.
As magical creatures, bugganes could not cross water or stand on hallowed ground.
The buggane's plan to wreck a ship was foiled by St Trinian, who guided it safely into Peel Harbour after the captain promised to build him a chapel.
Enraged, the buggane cried that St Trinian should never have a whole church in Ellan Vannin; three times the people roofed the chapel and three times the buggane tore it off.

The fairies sometimes called on bugganes to punish those who offended them; the Glen Maye buggane would have thrown a lazy housewife into a waterfall for baking after sunset had she not cut her apron strings to escape.
According to the French article, Irish legend says the Calf Sound south of the Isle of Man was formed in a fight between the Irish giant Finn Mac Cumaill and a buggane.
The Dutch article also calls the buggane a large ogre-like being of Manx mythology.

bungisngis.depicted_variant: Bungisngis, a Philippine humanoid giant: exactly ONE eye in the middle of its forehead, large exposed teeth, exactly TWO long tusks, and an exaggerated thick upper lip held low so its face is readable. Two arms and two legs, modest waist cloth, tropical woodland. No second or third eye.

basis_claims.statement: The bungisngis is a one-eyed giant of Philippine folklore said to live in Meluz, Orion, Bataan and Batangas and always laughing; its name comes from Cebuano ngisi, 'to giggle'.
This humanlike giant has always-visible large teeth, an upper lip covering its face when thrown back, two long tusks, and a single mid-forehead eye offset by sharp hearing.

In the Filipino tale The Three Friends: the Monkey, the Dog and the Carabao, the giant lifts the carabao and throws it knee-deep into the ground; though strong, it is easily outwitted and panics, and the Monkey's tricks lead to its death.

bunzi.depicted_variant: Bunzi in the Kongo serpent-water-spirit form: one continuous MULTICOLORED snake body with natural snake head, iridescent rainbow scales and no limbs, beside a Kongo river at sunset. No feathers, human torso or dragon wings.

basis_claims.statement: Bunzi is a serpent water spirit and goddess of rain in traditional Kongo religion first venerated by the Woyo of the Kingdom of Ngoyo.
Bunzi is depicted as a multicolored serpent rewarding worshippers with abundant harvest, appearing at sunset.
When Mboze gave birth, Bunzi was born in the form of a baby serpent.
Venerated in Democratic Republic of the Congo and Republic of the Congo.
Bunzi took on her mother's rain-bringing power.
According to the oral tradition of the Kongo people, Bunzi is the daughter of Mboze, the Great Mother and wife of Kuitikuiti.

busaw.depicted_variant: Busaw, the Philippine ghoul in the described form: one humanlike adult night spirit with POINTED TEETH, HOOKED NAILS and a LONG TONGUE, wearing a modest worn garment under a large tree near a quiet cemetery. No corpses or gore, no horns or bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: The busaw is a legendary creature resembling humans, raising animals and root crops, but its favourite food is humans, leaving skeletons around its home.

The busaw was an evil ghoul and corpse thief, human-seeming by day, listening for death at night, living in large trees near cemeteries, with pointed teeth, hooked nails and a long tongue; it replaced corpses with banana trunks, turned them into pigs and ate them.
To ward off the busaw, corpses should be washed with vinegar and strong-smelling herbs; salt also deters it.
The bal-bal is associated with the aswang, amalanhig and busaw, all flesh-eaters counted among the most feared creatures in the Philippines.

caballo-marino-chilote.depicted_variant: Caballo Marino Chilote: one horse-like aquatic animal with an unusually long HORSE SNOUT, GOLDEN MANE, FOUR clearly fin-like paws and a LONG FISH TAIL. Swimming underwater near the Chilean coast. No normal horse hooves, no mermaid torso or human head.

basis_claims.statement: The Caballo Marino Chilote ("Chilote sea horse") is an aquatic creature of Chilote mythology in Chile that resembles the hippocampus.
Legend says it is invisible and can only be seen by those with magical powers.
It looks like a normal horse but with a longer snout, golden mane, four fin-like paws and a long fish-like tail.
They exist in various sizes, from dwarfs to giants.
The Brujo Chilote (a sorcerer) rides it to reach the Caleuche ghost ship.

caballucos-del-diablu.depicted_variant: One Caballuco del Diablu in the documented RED Percheron-horse variant: an enormous red horse with BLACK mane and exactly TWO long transparent DAMSELFLY WINGS, galloping above fading Saint John's Eve bonfire embers in Cantabria. Four horse legs, no feathered wings, no insect body.

basis_claims.statement: The Caballucos del Diablu (Cantabrian for '(little) horses of the devil') is a myth of the mythology of Cantabria in northern Spain.
On St John's Eve (23 June), when people light bonfires to cleanse their souls, Percheron horses with damselfly wings, black manes and foaming mouths rise among the ashes.
These stallions are the souls of sinners doomed to roam Cantabria forever, who come to vent a year of sins in a roaring burst of fire and terrifying screams.
The red horse was a moneylender who tricked farmers out of their property, the white a miller who robbed his master, the black a deceiving hermit, and the yellow a corrupt judge.
The Devil himself is said to ride the red fire-breathing steed, the strongest, which leads the raid, while other demons ride the rest.
Their stamping is so strong that their horseshoes leave prints on rocks as if on freshly ploughed soil.
The Caballucos pounce on anyone they meet; the only protection is a bunch of vervain picked the day before, or placed by St John's fire, which they will not approach.
Sometimes, tired and resting, their saliva drips to the ground and turns into gold ingots; whoever takes them becomes very rich but goes straight to hell after death.
According to the Spanish article, in Cantabrian folk tradition the Caballucos del Diablu are seven beings looking like big dragonflies, with long transparent wings, flying the night sky.
The Esperanto article also calls them seven big dragonflies appearing on the night of 23 June.

cabra-cabriola.depicted_variant: Cabra Cabriola: one GOAT-like beast with curved goat horns, four goat legs and sharp visible TEETH, breathing a short plume of FIRE in an Iberian rocky landscape. No children or victims, no dragon wings, no human torso.

basis_claims.statement: The cabra cabriola ("leaping nanny goat") is a bogeyman of Portuguese myth told to children, also known elsewhere in Iberia and Brazil.
It is imagined as a fire-breathing, sharp-toothed, goat-like, child-eating beast.
It is a bogeyman that frightens children into good behavior.

cadejo.depicted_variant: Cadejo in a CALM dog-spirit form: one large doglike quadruped with clearly luminous BLUE EYES and dark coarse fur, on a Central American forest road at night. No red eyes in this calm variant, no horns, no human torso.

basis_claims.statement: The cadejo is a supernatural spirit of Central American folklore of indigenous origin, a dog-like creature with blue eyes when calm and red when hostile.
Legend says it wanders lonely roads at night.
The white cadejo protects travelers, while the black cadejo tries to kill them.

capelobo.depicted_variant: Capelobo in the animal variant: one TAPIR-like quadruped with LONG BLACK HAIR and a DOG-like snout, four sturdy legs, in an Amazonian forest of Brazil. No human body, no anteater snout mixed into this chosen variant, no horns.

basis_claims.statement: The Capelobo is a part-animal creature of Brazilian mythology with the snout of a pig, dog or giant anteater, depending on region, told in Pará or Maranhão.
It is feared as a man-eater, specifically a blood-sucker and brain-eater.
In the popular Xingu River basin version, the Capelobo has an animal form and a humanoid form.
In animal form it resembles a long, black-haired tapir with a dog or pig snout.
The Maranhão version is called Cupelobo and reputedly has a giant anteater snout.
The Capelobo is described as a blood-sucker and likened to the werewolf Lobisomem, or considered a sub-variant of it.
The only way to defeat it is to shoot it in the navel, which is covered in long fur.
The Capelobo screams a lot to announce itself, like the Mapinguari and the Pé de Garrafa.

catoblepas.depicted_variant: Catoblepas in the cape-buffalo-like description: one large buffalo-like quadruped whose exceptionally HEAVY HEAD hangs very LOW almost to the ground, thick dark hide, bovine horns and a stocky body. Rocky wetland setting. No upright proud head, no wings or human face.

basis_claims.statement: The catoblepas is a legendary creature of Aethiopia first described by Pliny the Elder and later Claudius Aelianus.
One description likens it to a cape buffalo whose heavy head always hangs down; its stare or breath could kill.
It is often thought to be based on encounters with wildebeest.

centaur.depicted_variant: One adult male Greek CENTAUR: human head, torso and two human arms joined at the waist to a complete HORSE body with FOUR horse legs and one horse tail. Modest cloth on human waist. Greek woodland. No separate human legs, no horse head, no wings.

basis_claims.statement: A centaur is a human-horse hybrid in Greek mythology.
Its head, arms, and torso are human, joined to a horse's body and legs.
Centaurs represented barbarism and chaos in Greek art.
Centaurs were believed to inhabit the forests of Thessaly.
Chiron was a centaur known for his wisdom.
Chiron mentored Jason, Peleus, Asclepius, Aristaeus, and Achilles.
At Peirithoos's wedding, centaurs fought the Lapiths and tried to abduct the bride.
Pholos was a centaur who hosted Hercules.

cerberus.depicted_variant: Cerberus in the three-headed variant: ONE large dog body, FOUR dog legs, exactly THREE clearly separated DOG HEADS on three necks, and a SINGLE SNAKE TAIL ending in one small serpent head. Guarding a dark Greek underworld cave. No lion heads, no extra body or wings.

basis_claims.statement: Cerberus is a three-headed dog guarding the underworld entrance in Greek mythology.
Cerberus seized those who tried to escape the underworld.
Cerberus is the child of Typhon and Echidna.
Cerberus was known as the Hound of Hades.
Hesiod described Cerberus as having fifty heads.
Depictions vary in head count and may give Cerberus a snake tail.
Hercules's twelfth labor was to bring Cerberus out of Tartarus.
Hades allowed Hercules to take Cerberus if he subdued him without weapons.
Hercules returned Cerberus to Hades after presenting him to Eurystheus.
Orpheus charmed Cerberus with his lyre in the underworld.

cha-kla.depicted_variant: Cha Kla in its recorded animal form: one black coarse-furred feline-like night creature with fur visibly growing UPWARD and FORWARD, BLOOD-RED eyes, in a shadowy Southeast Asian woodland clearing. No horns or wings; show fur direction clearly, no smooth glossy cat coat.

basis_claims.statement: Cha kla is recorded in the Ayutthaya-period Three Seals Law Code, over 300 years old, alongside beings such as the krasue, under the name cha la.
Cha kla's fur is pitch black, coarse and dull, growing backwards upward and forward, its eyes blood-red; it emerges only at night, fears humans and flees to its burrow when seen.
According to legend, cha kla has a deadly aura; merely seeing or touching it can cause death.

cheval-gauvin.depicted_variant: Cheval Gauvin, one sinister but anatomically normal HORSE of French Jura folklore, with one horse head, four hooved legs, mane and tail, standing by a dark stream in the forest. No wings, horns or human head; no rider.

basis_claims.statement: The Cheval Gauvin ('Gauvin horse') is a legendary evil horse of Franche-Comté, France, and the Jura Mountains of Switzerland, which wanders along streams, through forests and graveyards and tries to kill its riders by drowning them or throwing them into an abyss.
A legend of this horse was first collected at Chamblay by Désiré Monnier, who published it in 1854.
In Switzerland the horse gallops through villages and carries off young girls; one legend makes it the mount of the medieval lord Amauri III de Joux.
A harbinger of death, the Gauvin horse seems to have served as a children's bogeyman; perhaps a transformed goblin, it is one of many legendary Jura horses.
It shares its name with Gawain, the famous Round Table knight and nephew of King Arthur.
According to the French article, a woman's account of meeting it in the Chamblay cemetery has been told and discussed since the 19th century.
The Spanish article also calls the Gauvin horse, chevau Gauvin in Jura dialect or tcheva Gâvïn in Franc-Comtois, a legendary evil horse of Franche-Comté and the Swiss Jura.

cheval-mallet.depicted_variant: Cheval Mallet in its WHITE HORSE variant: one beautiful WHITE horse visibly SADDLED and BRIDLED, with four horse legs and normal equine head and tail, alone at night on a rural path in western France. No rider, wings or unicorn horn.

basis_claims.statement: The Cheval Mallet or Malet is a fabulous evil horse of the folklore of the Vendée, Poitou and especially the Pays de Retz near Lac de Grand-Lieu, France.

It appeared at night as a beautiful white or black horse, saddled and bridled, tempting exhausted travellers; those who rode it were never seen again unless they carried the fare or a protective charm such as a St Benedict medal.
Saint-Lumine-de-Coutais held a feast of the Horse Merlette, Merlet or Mallet, a renewal festival with actors around an oak, one dressed as a horse; the Church opposed it and it was banned in 1791.

According to the French article it is seen as the Devil's instrument or Satan himself, perhaps derived from Sleipnir and the Wild Hunt, and its legend is like those of other fabulous horses such as Lou Drapé or the blanque jument.
The name Mallet, corrupted to Merlet, may come from mail, 'trunk' or 'case', in old Celtic languages.
The Spanish article likewise calls the Cheval Mallet a mythical horse and evil being of Vendée folklore.

chi-mythology.depicted_variant: Chi in the HORNLESS DRAGON variant of Chinese tradition: one long scaled serpent-like dragon with four small clawed legs and an elongated dragon head, with visibly smooth head bearing NO horns or antlers, among Chinese mountain rocks. No wings or human face.

basis_claims.statement: Chi can denote a hornless dragon or mountain demon in Chinese mythology.
Hornless dragons were common motifs in ancient Chinese art.
The Shuowen Jiezi contains definitions for characters related to chi.

chickcharney.depicted_variant: Chickcharney, a feathered Bahamas woodland creature: one small upright birdlike being with RED EYES, TWO bird feet each showing exactly THREE TOES, and one LONG PREHENSILE TAIL curling around a branch. One bird head, feathered body. No mammalian fur or humanoid torso.

basis_claims.statement: The chickcharney is a legendary creature of the folklore of Andros in the Bahamas.
They are mischievous feathered creatures with red eyes, three toes per foot and long prehensile tails.
They live in pine forests and curse or bless travelers depending on how they are treated.

chimera-mythology.depicted_variant: The Greek Chimera: ONE lion body with FOUR lion legs and exactly THREE different heads: a LION head at the front, a GOAT head rising from its upper back, and a SNAKE head at the END OF ITS SERPENT TAIL. Greek rocky landscape. No extra separate body, no bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: The Chimera is a fire-breathing hybrid creature in Greek myth.
The three-headed Khimaira ravaged the Lycian countryside.
Its body combined lion, goat and serpent parts.
Echidna is named the mother of Chimaera in the Theogony.
Pegasus and Bellerophon slew Chimaera.
King Iobates ordered Bellerophon to slay the beast.
Bellerophon rode Pegasos into battle.
One version tells of a lead-tipped lance melting in its throat.
Pseudo-Apollodorus says Bellerophon shot the Chimera from the air.
The Greek name Chimaera means she-goat.
The Chimera had three heads.
The Theoi summary names Typhaon and Echidna as its parents.
Some later classical writers interpreted Chimera as a Lycian volcano metaphor.
Natural methane flames in western Lycia have been associated with its fiery breath.
Apollodorus reports Typhon and Echidna as its parents.

chonchon.depicted_variant: Chonchon in Mapuche folklore: ONE detached HUMAN HEAD with feathers, exactly TWO enormous EARS acting as wings, and two small TALONS beneath the head. Flying above a Chilean woodland at night. No full human torso, no bat wings replacing the ears, no extra heads.

basis_claims.statement: The Chonchon is a mythical creature of Mapuche religion and the folk mythologies of Chile and southern Argentina.
According to Mapuche myth the flying head comes from someone, usually a woman, who makes a pact with a sorcerer; her head detaches at night, sprouts wings and flies off.
There is supposedly a secret underground place called the reni where she flies to join her coven.
The kalku wizard himself can turn into the flying head.
To become a chonchon, the kalku anoints his throat with a magical cream.
The chonchon is a human head with feathers and talons; its huge ears act as wings for flying on moonless nights.
This form grants extra powers, including drinking the blood of the sick or sleeping.
Ordinary people can still hear its cry, "tue tue tue", taken as a dire omen of a loved one's death.
According to Jorge Luis Borges's Book of Imaginary Beings, the chonchon shows itself only to sorcerers; others only hear its cry.

chupacabra.depicted_variant: Chupacabra in the documented SOUTHWESTERN US variant: one hairless DOG/COYOTE-like quadruped with wrinkled grey skin, pointed canine ears, narrow snout, four legs and one thin tail. Dry scrub country. No Puerto Rican reptile spikes, bat wings or alien humanoid body.

basis_claims.statement: It is said to prey on livestock such as goats, chickens, dogs, and cats.
Accounts report it kills victims by puncturing the neck and consuming blood.
Descriptions of the creature vary considerably by region.
In Puerto Rico and Hispanic America, it is portrayed as a bipedal reptilian or alien entity.
In the Southwestern US, it is typically described as a hairless dog or coyote.
First widely publicized sightings emerged in Puerto Rico in 1995.
Since then, alleged sightings have been reported from Maine to Chile.
The name Chupacabras literally translates to goat-sucker in Spanish.
In 1975, unexplained livestock deaths in Moca were attributed to El Vampiro de Moca.
Comedian Silverio Pérez coined the term chupacabras shortly after 1995 reports.
Reports of sightings proliferated in the mid-1990s in various locations.
In April 2000, roughly one hundred farm animals were found dead in Calama, Chile.
During early 2002, cattle mutilation reports emerged in Argentina.
In July 2004, a rancher killed a creature resembling a hairless dog in Elmendorf, Texas.

cockatrice.depicted_variant: Cockatrice: a ROOSTER HEAD including a bright comb and wattles, joined to a reptilian serpentine body with exactly TWO legs and TWO bat-like wings, one long reptilian tail. European stone ruin. No four legs, no ordinary chicken body, no human head.

basis_claims.statement: A cockatrice is a mythical beast, essentially a two-legged dragon, wyvern or serpent-like creature with a rooster's head.

Laurence Breiner called it 'an ornament in the drama and poetry of the Elizabethans'; it was prominent in English thought and myth for centuries, and by legend hatches from a chicken egg incubated by a toad or snake.
The first English mention is in John Wycliffe's 14th-century Bible translation, used for various Hebrew words for asp and adder in Isaiah 11, 14 and 59.
The cockatrice came to be equated with the basilisk when the basiliscus in Bartholomeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (c. 1260) was translated by John Trevisa as cockatrice (1397).
The cockatrice can kill by touch, breath or a glance, called in literature 'the death-darting eye of Cockatrice'.
Late-medieval bestiaries repeat that the weasel alone is immune to its glance, and it was thought to die instantly on hearing a rooster crow.
A cock's egg was thought to hatch a cockatrice, which could be prevented by throwing the egg over the house without letting it hit the house.
According to the French article, the cocatrix (also coquatrix or caucatrix) has a rooster's head, bat's wings and a serpent's or cock's body.
Some sources say the cocatrix was 'born by accident at the end of the 12th century and died in the mid-17th, a victim of science'.
According to the Japanese article, it hatches from a rooster's egg incubated by a toad; the rooster is 7 years old and the toad broods it for 9 years.

colo-colo-mythology.depicted_variant: Colo Colo in its mature FEATHERED RAT variant: one rat-shaped small creature with a RAT head, four rat legs and one long rat tail, but the BODY is visibly covered in FEATHERS rather than ordinary fur. Chilean woodland. No rooster head, no wings or serpent body.

basis_claims.statement: The Colo Colo is an evil rat-like creature of Mapuche mythology.
It nests near homes, sneaks in and drains blood or saliva from sleepers, causing weakness or tuberculosis.
It hatches from a stunted "rooster's egg"; the young is snake- or lizard-like and later becomes a feathered rat.
A wildcat is also called "colocolo", perhaps related to the lore's origin.

cressie.depicted_variant: Cressie, a roughly fifteen-foot DARK BROWN EEL from Newfoundland legend: one long sleek eel body, natural eel head and low continuous fin, swimming in a clear freshwater lake. No snake horns, no limbs or dragon wings.

basis_claims.statement: In Canadian folklore, Cressie is an eel-like lake monster said to live in Crescent Lake, Robert's Arm, Newfoundland and Labrador.
The name blends Crescent Lake and Nessie, the Loch Ness Monster's nickname.
It has been described as a large dark brown eel about 15 feet long with a long, sleek body.
Sightings of Cressie began in the 1950s and continue today.
Some link it to earlier Indigenous legends of the woodum haoot ("pond devil") or haoot tuwedyee ("swimming demon").
Others caution that this link seems copied from source to source without verification.
There are no photographs of Cressie; all information relies on local oral history.
On July 9, 1991, Fred Parsons and his wife reported a large snakelike creature swimming in Crescent Lake.

cuelebre.depicted_variant: Cuelebre, an enormous WINGED SERPENT dragon of northern Spain: one continuous scaly serpent body with one reptilian head and exactly TWO BAT-LIKE WINGS, coiled at a cave entrance near old treasure. No legs, no feathered wings or human body.

basis_claims.statement: Cuélebre (Asturian) or Culebre (Cantabrian) is a legendary creature of northern Spain, a giant winged serpent-dragon that lives in caves, guards treasure and often holds anjanas or xanas captive.
Over time they age, their scales grow impenetrable and bat-like wings grow; though immortal, they finally leave their homeland and fly to a mythical paradise, Mar Cuajada, beyond the sea.
They seldom move except to eat cattle and people, and can be killed by feeding them a red-hot stone or a loaf filled with pins.
Its spit is believed to turn into a magic stone that heals many diseases.
In Asturian and Cantabrian folklore, on Midsummer night (San Juan) its spells fail so the brave can challenge it, and whoever defeats it may marry the xana and take its treasure.
But in Cantabrian lore, on Saint Bartholomew's Night the cuélebre grows stronger and vents its wrath on humans.
The German article also calls the cuélebre a giant winged snake-like dragon of Asturian and Cantabrian mythology.
According to the German article, their lamed wings gradually grow into the body, and they mostly lie motionless except to eat cattle or people.
According to the Japanese article, the dragon lives mainly in forests, underground caves and springs, its scales so hard that even bullets bounce off, with wings it can fly with.
For the cuélebre of the Brañaseca cave in Cudillero, villagers reportedly fed it corn or rye bread so it would not eat their livestock.
Not every cuélebre is fierce; some are said to look after the xana, the blonde water fairy.

curupira.depicted_variant: Curupira, a small humanlike Amazon forest guardian with flame-red hair and two backward-pointing feet. Final rear three-quarter view: back, hips and knees face away into the forest while toes of both feet face the viewer, opposite the body direction. Modest woven wrap, no actual fire or animal torso.

basis_claims.statement: Curupira is a forest spirit in the myths of Tupí-Guaraní-speaking areas of Brazil, Paraguay and the Guyanas.
It is a guardian of the forests that punishes people for overcutting.
The Curupira's feet point backwards, so its footprints mislead trackers in the opposite direction.
The earliest recorded mention of the Curupira was by Joseph of Anchieta on 30 May 1560 in São Vicente, São Paulo.
According to early Jesuits in São Paulo, the Curupira was a feared being that left gruesomely scarred bodies and was appeased with offerings.
Under European influence the figure changed into a more mischievous trickster spirit.
Some say it has blue or green teeth.
The name Curupira means "covered in wounds or blisters".
Some commentators consider the Curupira and the Caipora the same being; others say they differ.
It is regarded as the protector of forests and wild animals.
Other described features are flame-red or fiery hair.

dahu.depicted_variant: Dahu in its shorter-LEFT-legs variant: one chamois-like Alpine goat-antelope with two small curved horns and FOUR legs, the LEFT SIDE legs conspicuously SHORTER than the right side. Standing across a steep hillside with short legs on the uphill side and long legs on the downhill side. No extra limbs or wings.

basis_claims.statement: The dahu may have been inspired by the chamois, a small horned goat-antelope once common in European mountains, and also resembles the ibex.
Its main feature is that the legs on one side of its body are shorter than on the other, to help it stand and walk on steep slopes.
So there are two kinds: the laevogyrous dahu, with shorter left legs, circles the mountain anticlockwise, and the dextrogyre dahu, with shorter right legs, clockwise.
Supposedly, when the dahu turns towards an imitated call, it loses its balance and rolls down the slope to the person with the sack.
According to the French article, the dahu is usually brought up in the countryside as a joke on naive people or city folk unfamiliar with mountain wildlife.

dawon.depicted_variant: Dawon in the explicitly attested LION variant, Durga's mount shown alone: one majestic natural LION with a full mane, four lion legs and a tufted lion tail in an Indian woodland. No tiger stripes or composite anatomy, no rider or deity.

basis_claims.statement: Dawon is a lion or tiger serving as Durga's mount in Hindu tradition.
The article also calls it Somnandi.
In Durga's fight with Mahishasura one of her feet rests on Somnandi.
The article identifies Durga's lion with Vishnu in a Kalika Purana account.
Ghatokbahini in Bengali art is depicted as a half lion half tiger hybrid.
The article links Dawon to a sacred Tibetan tiger later called Gdon.

delphyne.depicted_variant: Delphyne, the monstrous SHE-SERPENT of Delphi: one giant natural snake head and continuous thick scaly snake body, coiled among Greek limestone rocks. No human head, no wings, no legs or multiple heads.

basis_claims.statement: Delphyne is, in some accounts, the name of the monstrous serpent Apollo killed at Delphi.
In the earliest account, the Homeric Hymn to Apollo (6th century BC), the god kills a nameless she-serpent later called Delphyne.
According to the Suda, Delphi was named after Delphyne.

demon-cat.depicted_variant: Demon Cat in the Capitol ghost legend: one giant anatomically CAT-like BLACK cat, swollen to the size of a tiger, within a shadowy historic stone corridor. One cat head, two ears, four feline legs and one tail. No horns, wings or humanoid body.

basis_claims.statement: The Demon Cat is a ghost cat of American folklore said to haunt government buildings in Washington, D.C.
It is said to haunt the White House and the United States Capitol.
Cats were brought into the basement tunnels of the Capitol Building to catch rats and mice.
Legend says the Demon Cat is one of those cats that never left, even after death.
According to legend, the cat is seen before presidential elections and tragedies in Washington, D.C.
It is described as a black or tabby cat the size of an ordinary house cat.
Witnesses report that the cat swells to "the size of a giant tiger" or an elephant.
In the 1890s the cat reportedly vanished inexplicably when some Capitol Hill guards fired at it.
According to Steve Livengood, chief tour guide of the U.S. Capitol Historical Society, the Capitol Police was notorious for hiring unqualified relatives and friends of Congressmen.
Livengood thinks the legend began when a drunken guard was licked by one of the Capitol's cats and mistook it for a giant cat.
According to legend, the Demon Cat appears before disasters; it was seen before the assassinations of John Kennedy and Abraham Lincoln and before the 1929 Wall Street crash.

dewey-lake-monster.depicted_variant: Dewey Lake Monster in its reported form: one enormous approximately TEN-FOOT hair-covered biped with a bulky humanoid-ape body, two long arms, two legs and brightly GLOWING EYES in Michigan woodland. No lake-serpent anatomy, no horns or bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: The creature is also known as Sister Lakes Sasquatch, similar to descriptions of Bigfoot.
Described as covered in hair, 10 feet tall, 500 pounds, with glowing eyes.
Attracted national attention in June 1964 following sightings by local residents.

dip-catalan-myth.depicted_variant: Dip, the Catalan black vampire dog: one shaggy BLACK DOG, distinctly LAME in ONE leg held slightly off the ground, one canine head and one dog tail, beside a Catalan rural track at night. No horns, no human torso, no victims.

basis_claims.statement: In Catalan myth the Dip is an evil black hellhound, the Devil's emissary, who sucks people's blood; like other Catalan demonic figures he is lame in one leg, and he appears on the arms of Pratdip.
The legend is very old: images of these vampire dogs appear on the Santa Marina de Pratdip altarpiece of 1602 and another of 1730 on a gold ground.
By legend these dogs sucked cattle's blood, went out only at night, and their victims included drunken night-owls leaving the village taverns.
The legend is thought to have been meant to frighten village drunkards out of further drinking.
By tradition the village's name comes from these dogs, said to have vanished in the 19th century, and a friendly-looking dip monument stands at the entrance to Pratdip.
According to the Spanish article, the village name comes from dip (Pratdip = 'meadow of dips'), and dip comes from Arabic for wolf.
There is no firm evidence or documented witness that this legend was actually told in the village.
According to the Catalan article, deriving the village name from the dips is folk etymology; Pratdip is actually a pre-Roman place name.
The dip is a kind of evil, hairy vampire dog, a devil's emissary lame in one leg, feeding on the blood of animals and people.

diting.depicted_variant: Diting in the documented composite form: ONE TIGER HEAD with DOG EARS and exactly ONE horn, ONE scaled DRAGON BODY, four hooved qilin-like animal feet and a LION TAIL with a tuft. Resting in a Chinese temple courtyard. No eagle beak, no turtle shell, no extra heads or wings.

basis_claims.statement: Diting is a divine creature and Ksitigarbha's steed in Chinese Buddhism.
Its form combines a tiger head, dragon body, lion tail, one horn, dog ears and qilin feet.
One legend identifies its origin as a white dog.
The dog accompanying Kim Gyo-gak is believed to become Diting after Ksitigarbha's enlightenment.
In Journey to the West Diting can distinguish the true Sun Wukong from the impostor.

dodomeki.depicted_variant: Dodomeki, a female-shaped Japanese yokai: one adult woman in a modest old Japanese robe with BOTH ARMS exposed only from elbow to wrist, her forearms visibly covered in MANY SMALL EYES. Natural human face with two eyes, black hair. No eyes on torso, no extra arms or wings.

basis_claims.statement: Dodomeki is a female-shaped Japanese yōkai with eye-covered arms.
Another name for it is todomeki.
Toriyama Sekien described it in the eighteenth century.
The eyes on its arms have been associated with the appearance of old coins.

european-dragon.depicted_variant: A European dragon in the attested medieval form: one huge horned scaly LIZARD-LIKE body, FOUR clawed legs, TWO leathery BAT WINGS, one long muscular tail and one dragon head breathing a short flame, outside a rocky treasure cave. No feathers, no wingless Chinese serpent form.

basis_claims.statement: The European dragon is a legendary creature of the folklore and mythology of Europe's overlapping cultures.
From the Early Middle Ages the European dragon is usually shown as a large, fire-breathing, scaly, horned, lizard-like creature with leathery bat-like wings and a long, muscular, grasping tail.
The typical dragon of Christian culture guards a cave or castle full of gold and treasure; an evil dragon is tied to a hero who tries to slay it, while a good one gives help or wise counsel.
In some accounts the hero Sigurð defeats Fáfnir by digging a pit, lying in wait and stabbing his heart with a sword as he passes over.
The Roman poet Virgil, in his poem Culex (lines 163–201), calls the great snake a shepherd fights both serpens and draco, showing the two words could probably mean the same thing in his day.
Roman dragons grew out of serpent-like Greek ones combined with Near Eastern dragons in the hybrid Hellenistic culture.

According to the French article, the word dragon comes from Ancient Greek drákōn, from dérkomai, 'to see, to stare', and Latin draco; in European tradition it is a winged creature with a lizard's tail and clawed feet.
Python, Ladon and the Lernaean Hydra are often counted as dragons, but ancient works show them only as serpents, sometimes giant or many-headed.
The terms worm (Germanic myth), wyrm (Anglo-Saxon) and wurm (Old High German) for dragon-like creatures also mean serpent.
According to the Japanese article, dragons whose forelegs are wings like a bird's or bat's are often called wyverns, while wingless ones are sometimes called worms.
In Japanese it is also called ryū; it resembles the Eastern dragon but is not directly related.

fish-man.depicted_variant: The Fish Man of Lierganes: one adult young HUMAN MAN with WHITE skin and THIN RED HAIR, a vertical strip of SCALES from throat toward belly and clearly visible small GILLS on the neck. Modest simple trousers. Near a northern Spanish river. Two arms, two human legs; no fish tail or full fish head.

basis_claims.statement: His story was examined by the Enlightenment writer Benito Jerónimo Feijoo, who claimed it was true.
According to Feijoo, Francisco de la Vega Casar of Liérganes worked as a carpenter in Bilbao until 1674, when on St John's Eve he went swimming with friends in the Bilbao estuary.
He was last seen swimming out to sea and was thought drowned.
Five years later, in 1679, fishermen in the Bay of Cádiz saw a strange creature caught in their nets, struggling to escape.

Once caught with bread, the creature proved to be a young man with white skin and thin red hair, but with a strip of scales from throat to belly and down his spine, and what looked like gills on his neck.
According to the Spanish article, the first account of the fish-man is in volume VI of Fray Benito Jerónimo Feijoo's Teatro crítico universal.

flaming-teeth.depicted_variant: Flaming Teeth, the Fijian giant: one immense HUMANLIKE giant with an open mouth revealing oversized TEETH glowing like BURNING LOGS, two arms and two legs, modest woven waist cloth, Fijian rocky shoreline. The teeth alone glow; no skull face or whole burning body.

basis_claims.statement: Flaming Teeth was a giant in Fijian lore whose teeth looked like burning logs.
The colossal monster terrorized villages by eating people and causing wide damage.

flatwoods-monster.depicted_variant: Flatwoods Monster in the reported form: one tall upright figure with a ROUND RED FACE surrounded by a pointed hood-like head outline like the ACE OF SPADES, small CLAW-LIKE hands and a body with CLOTHING-LIKE folds, in wooded West Virginia at dusk. No text or card symbol printed on head, no UFO or other characters.

basis_claims.statement: on September 12, 1952, in Flatwoods, brothers Edward and Fred May, accompanied by their friend Tommy Hyer, reported seeing a bright object cross the sky before landing on the property of farmer G.
Lemon said he aimed a flashlight in that direction and momentarily saw a tall 'man-like figure with a round, red face surrounded by a pointed, hood-like shape'.
The witnesses further claimed that the figure possessed 'small, claw-like hands', clothing-like folds, and 'a head that resembled the ace of spades'.

In 2000, paranormal investigator Joe Nickell suggested that the light was a meteor, while the creature may have been a barn owl perched in a tree whose shadows made it appear as a large humanoid figure.

flying-head.depicted_variant: Flying Head of Haudenosaunee/Wyandot folklore: one huge detached HUMAN HEAD with LONG DARK HAIR, TERRIBLE EYES and an enormous mouth of RAZOR-SHARP FANGS, floating above a northeastern American woodland. No torso, no enormous ear-wings, no explicit organs or gore.

basis_claims.statement: The Flying Head (also Big Head or the Great Head) is a cannibalistic spirit of Haudenosaunee and Wyandot mythology.
Flying Heads are ravenous spirits cursed with insatiable hunger.
They resemble a human head with long dark hair, "terrible eyes" and a large mouth of razor-sharp fangs.
In some versions it has bat wings at each cheek and bird-like talons.
In all versions it is larger than the tallest man, with a hide no weapon can pierce.
According to folklore, the Flying Head drove the original inhabitants near the source of the Hudson River in the Adirondack Mountains from their hunting grounds before Europeans came.

forest-bull.depicted_variant: Forest Bull of ancient bestiaries: one TAWNY bovine quadruped with a mouth that GAPES almost to the ears and TWO HORNS pointing in different directions to suggest their swiveling ability. Four bovine legs and one bull tail, dry African woodland. No human face, wings or extra horns.

basis_claims.statement: The Forest Bull is an animal of ancient and medieval bestiaries; according to Pliny the Elder they were fierce, tawny cattle of Ethiopia with mouths gaping to the ears and horns that, like a Yale's, could swivel any way.
According to Aelian they were called 'flesh eaters', the fiercest of all animals, twice the size of ordinary bulls and very fast.
No weapon could hurt them, as spears, arrows and even iron glanced off their hide.
To protect their flocks, local herdsmen dug deep ditches into which the bulls fell and choked on their own rage.
According to the Dutch article, the animal may be based on travellers' accounts of the African buffalo.

fouke-monster.depicted_variant: Fouke Monster in the reported form: one LARGE BIPED covered in LONG DARK HAIR, with an ape-like humanoid face, two arms and two legs, walking through southern Arkansas swamp woods. No horned deer head, no dragon tail or wings.

basis_claims.statement: The Fouke Monster is a large, hairy humanoid said to have been seen in Fouke and Miller County, Arkansas, in the early 1970s.
Reports from 1971 to 1974 described a large bipedal creature covered in long dark hair.

furaribi.depicted_variant: Furaribi in the documented DOG-FACED BURNING BIRD variant: one compact feathered BIRD BODY, TWO bird legs and TWO wings, with ONE DOG-LIKE FACE instead of a beak, surrounded by a soft flame aura. Old Japanese woodland at night. No human face, no four-legged dog body.

basis_claims.statement: Furaribi is a fiery yōkai represented in Japanese illustrated books.
Some artists picture a burning bird with a dog-like face.
Another old illustration shows a burning bird with a different face.
The books give little explanation, leaving its identity uncertain.

futakuchi-onna.depicted_variant: Futakuchi Onna in the two-mouthed variant: one adult Japanese woman with a NORMAL HUMAN FACE and one normal mouth, modest traditional robe and long BLACK HAIR. In a rear three-quarter view, her hair parts to reveal exactly ONE SECOND MOUTH with lips, teeth and tongue on the BACK OF HER HEAD. Show rear mouth clearly; no extra face or mouths on her body.

basis_claims.statement: Her second mouth is hidden behind her head under her hair.
The extra mouth is depicted with lips, teeth and a tongue.
The second mouth is often linked to a woman who eats very little.
In many stories she is the wife of a miser.
The extra mouth demands food and utters threats.

fuzhu-mythical-beast.depicted_variant: Fuzhu, one natural DEER-like creature with exactly FOUR distinct antler-like HORNS on its head, four slender deer legs and a deer tail, beside a flooded Chinese river plain. No wings, no three or five horns.

basis_claims.statement: Fuzhu is a Chinese mythological beast appearing in the Shanhaijing.
Its portrayal is a deer with four horns.
The creature is described as gentle and fond of cleanliness.
Its appearance is associated with periods of flooding.

gaasyendietha.depicted_variant: Gaasyendietha, the Seneca meteor dragon: one huge scaled SERPENT with one serpent head and a continuous body, rising over Lake Ontario with a subtle meteoric glow along its outline. No wings, no legs or feathered body; no literal spacecraft.

basis_claims.statement: Gaasyendietha, the "meteor dragon" of Seneca mythology, is a giant serpent living in the depths of Canadian rivers and lakes, especially Lake Ontario.
It could fly on a trail of fire and spew fire, so it is likened to European dragons.
The name "meteor dragon" refers to its supposed origin in a meteoroid that struck Earth.

gloucester-sea-serpent.depicted_variant: The Gloucester Sea Serpent in the historical reported form: one MASSIVE serpent-like animal with a succession of clearly visible HUMPS along its long back at the water surface off Cape Ann. One snake-like head, no legs or wings, a tiny unoccupied fishing boat for scale.

basis_claims.statement: The Gloucester sea serpent is a legendary creature reported seen around the coast of Gloucester, Massachusetts and Cape Ann.
The heyday of sightings began in August 1817 and continued into 1818–1819.
Described as a massive serpent-like creature with humps along its back, it was subject of encounters by fishermen.

goatman-urban-legend.depicted_variant: Goatman of Maryland in the goat-human hybrid form: one GOAT HEAD with goat ears, two curved horns and a beard, joined to a strong humanlike torso, two arms and two upright goat-like legs. Modest waist wrap, Maryland woodland. No wings, no horse body or bull head.

basis_claims.statement: Creature information Grouping Cryptid Origin Region Prince George's County, Maryland According to urban legend, Goatman is a creature resembling a goat-human hybrid often credited with canine deaths and purported to take refuge in the woods of Prince George's County, Maryland, United States.
In Lizama’s paper, the Goatman was said to be located on Tucker Road in Fort Washington, Maryland.

Later the same year, reporter Karen Hosler discovered Lizama’s project in the Maryland Folklife Archives and reported on it in the Prince George’s County News in October 1971, this time placing the Goatman near Fletchertown Road in Bowie, Maryland.
Additionally, this report covered the theory that the Goatman’s origins can be traced to the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center.

gaueko.depicted_variant: Gaueko in the recorded BLACK WOLF variant: one large BLACK WOLF with normal canine head, four wolf legs and a bushy tail, in a Basque forest at night. No horns, no humanlike body, no giant red eyes added.

basis_claims.statement: In Basque mythology Gaueko is the spirit of the night, who forbids certain work outside the house at night and especially punishes those who boast of not fearing the dark.
Some accounts make him a devil, others a jentil or pagan deity.
Sometimes he makes himself felt as a gust of wind, saying 'Gaua Gauekoarentzat, eguna egunezkoarentzat' (the night for Gaueko, the day for the day).
Sometimes he appears as a cow, sometimes as a monster.
In Basque, Gaueko literally means 'of the night'.
According to the French article, Gaueko's night is usually understood as from midnight to the first cockcrow, though it may also be bounded by the evening and morning Angelus.
His rule comes with a ban on leaving the protection of the home, guarded by household spirits; those who break it risk abduction or unexplained disappearance.
According to the Spanish article, he was pictured as an invisible presence, a black wolf (otsobeltza) sometimes standing on two legs, or another animal such as a cow, owl or sheep.
Like the goddess Mari, Gaueko could change shape and command the elements, though powerless against her, and he was feared for eating shepherds and sheep.
When people asked Mari for help against Gaueko, she blessed them with the light of her first daughter, Ilargi (the moon), but it was not enough and they asked again.

akugyo.depicted_variant: Akugyo in the SHINING-SCALED GIANT FISH variant: one immense natural FISH with an ordinary fish head, clearly fishlike fins and a caudal fin, its scales shining gently beneath Japanese coastal water. No fiery breath for this chosen variant, no eel body or horns.

basis_claims.statement: Akugyo is a sea monster in Japanese legend.
Accounts place these giant fish near the former Kibi Province.
Stories say they overturn ships and prey on sailors.
Different depictions give them fiery breath or shining scales.

alara-fairy.depicted_variant: Alara in the Lake Baikal appearance: one small GIRL-like fairy in a modest opaque dress with exactly TWO luminous BUTTERFLY WINGS, beside the clear cold waters of Lake Baikal. Humanlike arms and legs, no bird feathers, no adult sexualized appearance.

basis_claims.statement: Alara is a water fairy from Turkic mythology referenced in Siberian and Yakut folklore
Originated from Lake Baikal appearing as a little girl with butterfly wings of light
Her beauty and youth depend on water and must stay close to water sources
She has power to remove hate and greed from people's hearts
Those seeking help tie a colorful ribbon on a lakeside tree branch

anqa.depicted_variant: Anqa in the described Arabian bird form: one GOLDEN female mythical bird with a long neck, a HUMAN FACE, an avian body and exactly FOUR PAIRS OF WINGS (EIGHT distinct feathered wings) fanned into separate layers. Desert oasis. Two bird feet, no lion body, no extra heads.

basis_claims.statement: Anqa is a golden female mythical bird in pre-Islamic Arab mythology.
Anqa is said to be found where the sun sets.
The name Anqa is linked with meanings of a long or thick neck.
Anqa is portrayed as colorful, with a long neck, a human face, and four pairs of wings.
Al-Qazwini places Anqa alone on Mount Qaf.
Anqa is said to eat only elephants and large fish.
Anqa starts as God’s perfect creation and later becomes a plague in the hadith tradition cited by Iranica.

ahriman.depicted_variant: Ahriman in the documented SNAKE shapeshifting form: one dark natural snake with one reptilian head and a continuous scaled body, in a deep shadowy rocky Iranian landscape. No humanoid demon, no wings, horns or extra heads; this is specifically the snake manifestation.

basis_claims.statement: Ahriman is an evil spirit in Iranian tradition, Zoroastrianism, and Zurvanism, associated with darkness and chaos.
Angra Mainyu is another name for Ahriman.
The source places Ahriman in opposition to Spenta Mainyu and Ahura Mazda.
In Zurvanism, Zurvan gives birth to Ahura Mazda and Ahriman.
In the quoted account by Hinnells, Ahriman inhabits an abyss of endless northern darkness.
Ahriman can change form into a lizard, snake, or young man.
Ahriman’s aim is described as destroying Ahura Mazda’s creation.
Ahriman counters life with death and health with disease.
The account includes Gavaevodta, the Primordial Bull.
Gayomartan is also killed by Ahriman in that account.
Ahriman lies to the first human couple by claiming to be their creator.
His Avestan name is Angra Mainyu.
In the Gathas, angra mainyu is not yet a proper name.
Angra Mainyu falls into a stupor when Ahura Mazda recites Ahuna Vairya.
The introduction to Vendidad I describes sixteen lands created by Ahura Mazda and opposing plagues created by Angra Mainyu.

akuma-folklore.depicted_variant: Akuma in the documented Japanese figure: one humanlike spirit with a FIERY HEAD, FLAMING EYES and one SWORD held in a hand, modest dark garment, shadowy Japanese rocky setting. Two arms and two legs. No Western goat head or bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: Akuma is an evil spirit in Japanese folklore also called ma.
Early uses of the word akuma are mainly found in Buddhist texts.
The word also appears in literary works of the Heian period.
Akuma is depicted with a fiery head, flaming eyes, and a sword.
Seeing one is believed to herald misfortune.
It is said to possess people and cause natural disasters.
An old Japanese–English dictionary lists Akuma as a synonym for a demon or evil spirit.

almaz-mythical-beast.depicted_variant: Almaz in the documented FEMALE Caucasian forest-being variant: one adult humanlike woman with exceptionally long GOLDEN HAIR, modest draped clothing and a solemn expression, in a Caucasus forest. Her flowing hair is the distinguishing feature; no horns, wings or animal face.

basis_claims.statement: Almaz is a forest creature in Chechen, Ingush and Circassian folk belief, with magical power in its hair.
Male almaz are described as hairy and hideous with an axe embedded in the chest.
Females are described as beautiful with golden hair.
Removing or grabbing its hair can render an almaz helpless.

aloja-mythology.depicted_variant: Aloja in the nocturnal Catalan water-fairy variant: one adult woman with shimmering GOLDEN HAIR, EMERALD EYES and fine modest historical clothing, looking at her reflection in a lake on a full-moon night. Human legs, no fish tail, no butterfly wings.

basis_claims.statement: In Catalan mythology an aloja (also dona d'aigua, goja or paitida) is a female being living where there is fresh water, said to be able to turn into a water blackbird (dipper).
They are not immortal but can live for thousands of years and stay young.
The lakes where they bathe are said to boil with anger if a stranger enters; in Mallorca the most famous is Maria Enganxa, who lives in every well and cistern and hooks children who pass by.
They are nocturnal, with shimmering gold or red hair and emerald or deep blue eyes, wear fine clothes and like to see their reflection in lakes on full-moon nights.
In tales of marriage with humans the condition is often that the husband must not reveal his wife is a water-woman; if he does, she leaves and takes his fortune.
According to the Spanish article they are spirits favouring births and fertility, life-givers and renewers of nature, generally kindly though one should be careful on meeting them.
The word goja may come from Old Catalan or Occitan, meaning 'young maiden'.
They always live near cold blue waters: Pyrenean tarns, torrents and waterfalls, forest springs, pools, damp caves and underground streams and lakes.
They are a local adaptation of the nymphs as embodiments of nature's feminine forces.
The Aragonese article also says they live in the Pyrenees where there is water, such as springs, rivers, torrents or damp caves.

ama-no-fuchigoma.depicted_variant: Ama no Fuchigoma, the mythical horse of the Nihon Shoki: one normal majestic HORSE with one horse head, mane, FOUR hooved legs and a flowing tail, on a misty ancient Japanese woodland path. No rider, wings, horns or human face; do not invent unsupported special markings.

basis_claims.statement: Ama no Fuchigoma is a mythical horse in the Nihon Shoki.
Susanoo rides the horse in the myth.

akerbeltz.depicted_variant: Akerbeltz in the attested BLACK BILLY GOAT form: one black male goat with goat beard, TWO backward-curving goat horns, four cloven-hooved goat legs and a short goat tail near a Basque cave. No human torso, no bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: Akerbeltz or Aker (Basque aker, 'billy goat', and beltz, 'black') is a spirit of Basque folk mythology who lives inside the earth and has many elves as servants.
Today Akerbeltz is thought to have been an ancient deity who protected animals.
The inquisitor Pierre de Lancre, who hunted supposed witches in Labourd and Lower Navarre, wrote a book recording testimony about Akerbeltz.
One 'witch' testified that he had two faces, one in front and one behind.
According to the witch-hunters, Aker held a parody of the Catholic mass for his followers, who offered him eggs, bread and money.
Other beliefs make him protector of animals and houses, able to heal animals, and an image of fertility.
Because he was black, many Basques kept a black billy goat in the stable to protect the other animals.
He was said to dwell at the mouth of the Zugarramurdi caves, where elves, lamiak and witches met.
Pyrenean people believed witches, Akerbeltz and the devil could enter any house and take a billy goat's beard to make hail.
According to the French article, Aker or Akerbeltz is an evil underground genie in goat form who commands many genies and can raise storms.
The names of the Egyptian god Aker and the Basque Aker sound alike, though nothing is certain.
Akelarre or Akerlanda ('goat's meadow') is where the sabbath is held, and Aker presided over these revels with the witches (sorginak).
According to the Spanish article, Christianity identified Akerbeltz with the devil presiding over the akelarres, the witches' gatherings.
Other inquisitors likened him to an enormous dog or a big ox, perhaps related to the myth of the Aatxe.

ahuizotl-mythology.depicted_variant: Ahuizotl, the Aztec water dog: one small dog-sized waterproof-furred quadruped with a canine-like head and a long PREHENSILE TAIL whose END is a clearly visible HUMANLIKE HAND with five fingers. Four animal legs, Aztec-region freshwater bank. No extra hands on torso, no serpent head on tail.

basis_claims.statement: The ahuizotl is a legendary creature of Aztec mythology said to lure people to their deaths.
The ruler of the same name took it as his emblem, and it was called a "friend of the rain gods".
Hernán Cortés once reported to the King of Castile that one of his men had been killed by an ahuizotl.
It is described as the size of a small dog, with waterproof fur.
The ahuizotl is recorded in Book 11 of the Florentine Codex.
In some versions the gods Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue sent it to collect the souls of mortals they favoured.
By most accounts the ahuizotl snatched people from the water's edge to feast on their eyes, nails and teeth.
The ahuizotl was said to snatch its prey with the hand at the end of its tail.
The name comes from Nahuatl and roughly means "water dog".
The Aztec ruler Auítzotl took his name from the creature and saw it as his protective figure.

akashita.depicted_variant: Akashita/Akaguchi in the depicted Japanese form: one shaggy beastlike head and visible CLAWS emerging from a dense BLACK CLOUD, with a very large clearly RED TONGUE, positioned over an old wooden Japanese FLOODGATE. Most body concealed by black cloud. No full human body or dragon wings.

basis_claims.statement: BYU describes akaguchi amid a black cloud with claws and red tongue.
BYU says akaguchi is better known as akashita.
Akaguchi is depicted over a floodgate.
One account says akaguchi punishes water thieves.
A Tsugaru water-dispute tale appears in a 1974 book.
Sekien’s akashita was later retrofitted to the water-dispute story.

griffin.depicted_variant: Griffin in its documented eagle-lion hybrid form: ONE EAGLE HEAD with a hooked beak and small pointed ears, TWO large FEATHERED EAGLE WINGS, joined to a muscular LION BODY with four legs and one long LION TAIL. Eaglelike taloned forefeet and lion hind paws, in rocky Scythian mountains guarding a small pile of old gold. No human torso, no lion head, no horse hindquarters or bat wings.

basis_claims.statement: The griffin is a hybrid with an eagle's head and wings and a lion's body.
In Greek accounts, griffins guarded gold in the mountains of Scythia.
The one-eyed Arimaspians were said to fight griffins for gold.
Griffins appeared in ancient Greek art and later in medieval bestiaries and heraldry.
The griffin was a favored motif on ancient Greek bronze vessels.
On a throne leg documented by the Met, the griffin served as a symbol of royalty.
Griffin imagery appeared in Egyptian and Middle Eastern art around 3000 BCE.
In pre-Islamic Iran the griffin was understood as a vehicle of ascension.
Pausanias described griffins as lion-like beasts with eagle beaks and wings.

adze-folklore.depicted_variant: Firefly form only; luminous beetle beside a door crack at night.

basis_claims.statement: In the wild, the adze takes the form of a firefly, transforming into human shape upon capture with power to possess humans.
basis_claims.statement_id: Di alam liar Adze berwujud kunang-kunang, berubah menjadi manusia jika ditangkap dan memiliki kekuatan merasuki manusia.
basis_claims.quote: In the wild, the adze takes the form of a firefly, though it will transform into human shape upon capture. When in human form, the adze has the power to possess humans.

basis_claims.statement: In firefly form, the adze enters homes at night through keyholes to suck blood from sleeping victims.
basis_claims.statement_id: Dalam wujud kunang-kunang, Adze masuk melalui lubang kunci dan celah pintu malam hari untuk menghisap darah saat tidur.
basis_claims.quote: In firefly form, the adze would travel through keyholes, cracks in walls, or under closed doors at night. Once in the home, it would suck blood from people as they slept, making them fall sick and die. Tales of the creature and its effects were probably an attempt to describe the potentially deadly effects of mosquitoes and malaria. There is no defense against an adze.

ghillie-dhu.depicted_variant: Dark-haired male fairy in leaves and moss

moddey-dhoo.depicted_variant: Peel Castle large black shaggy spaniel

basis_claims.statement: Äbädä is a harmless forest spirit of Turkic mythology that looks like an old woman and also appears in the mythologies of Siberian peoples.
basis_claims.statement_id: Äbädä adalah roh hutan yang tidak berbahaya dalam mitologi Turkik, berwujud perempuan tua, dan juga dikenal dalam mitologi bangsa-bangsa Siberia.
basis_claims.quote: is an innocent forest spirit in Turkic mythology. It looks like an old woman. Äbädä also is represented in mythologies of Siberian peoples.

basis_claims.statement: In Turkic and Tatar mythology Əbədə is a tree spirit that lives in forests, harms no one and looks like an old woman.
basis_claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Turki dan Tatar, Əbədə adalah jin pohon yang tinggal di hutan, tidak mencelakai manusia, dan berwujud perempuan tua.
basis_claims.quote: Əbədə — türk və tatar mifologiyasında ağac cini. Meşələrdə yaşayır. İnsanlara zərər verməz. Yaşlı bir qadın görümündədir.

basis_claims.statement: The rustling of dry leaves on the forest floor is the sound of her footsteps.
basis_claims.statement_id: Gemeresik daun kering di tanah hutan adalah suara langkah kakinya.
basis_claims.quote: Meşələrdə yerlərdəki qurumuş ağac yarpaqlarından gələn çıtırtılar onun ayaq səsləridir.

basis_claims.statement: Akateko is a yōkai told of in the Aomori area.
basis_claims.statement_id: Akateko adalah yōkai yang diceritakan di daerah Aomori.
basis_claims.quote: An akateko (赤手児; lit. "red child's hand") is a yōkai, or Japanese monster, from the folklore of Aomori Prefecture, specifically in the city of Hachinohe.

basis_claims.statement: It is described as a red child's hand hanging from a tree.
basis_claims.statement_id: Makhluk itu digambarkan sebagai tangan merah anak kecil yang muncul dari pohon.
basis_claims.quote: The monster is described as the red, disembodied hand of a small child descending from a Japanese honey locust tree.

basis_claims.statement: The batibat is a vengeful demon of Ilocano folklore, called bangungot in Tagalog folklore, taking the form of an ancient, grossly obese, tree-dwelling female spirit.
basis_claims.statement_id: Batibat adalah setan pendendam dalam cerita rakyat Ilokano, disebut bangungot dalam cerita rakyat Tagalog, berwujud roh perempuan tua yang sangat gemuk penghuni pohon.
basis_claims.quote: The Batibat is a vengeful demon found in Ilocano folklore. In Tagalog folklore, the creature is called Bangungot. The batibat takes the form of an ancient, grotesquely obese, tree-dwelling female spirit.

basis_claims.statement: Batibat usually meet humans when their trees are felled, especially when made into a house post, and then inhabit what is left of the tree.
basis_claims.statement_id: Batibat biasanya bersentuhan dengan manusia ketika pohonnya ditebang, terutama bila dijadikan tiang rumah, lalu ia menghuni sisa pohonnya.
basis_claims.quote: They usually come in contact with humans when the trees in which they reside are felled and are made homeless, especially when their tree is made into a support post for a house.

basis_claims.statement: The boobrie is a shapeshifter of west-coast Scottish lochs, a giant water bird like a cormorant or great northern diver, or a water bull.
basis_claims.statement_id: Boobrie pengubah wujud di danau (lochs) pantai barat Skotlandia (Scotland), burung air raksasa mirip kormoran atau great northern diver, juga banteng air; di Britania Raya.
basis_claims.quote: The boobrie is a mythological shapeshifting entity inhabiting the lochs of the west coast of Scotland. It commonly adopts the appearance of a gigantic water bird resembling a cormorant or great northern diver, but it can also materialise in the form of various other mythological creatures such as a water bull.

basis_claims.statement: A huge seabird like the cormorant or Plongeon huard, white-spotted, bellowing, devouring sheep and cattle.
basis_claims.statement_id: Burung laut raksasa mirip kormoran atau Plongeon huard, berbintik putih, melenguh, melahap domba dan sapi.
basis_claims.quote: Il est communément décrit comme un énorme oiseau de mer, ressemblant au cormoran ou au Plongeon huard (Gavia immer), mais dont le corps serait taché de blanc et qui serait capable de mugir. Sa corpulence lui permet de dévorer des moutons et des bovins.

basis_claims.statement: Lives in mountain pools and waterfalls; a spirit as a grey or black white-maned horse, sometimes winged.
basis_claims.statement_id: Menghuni kolam gunung dan air terjun; roh berwujud kuda kelabu atau hitam bersurai putih, kadang bersayap.
basis_claims.quote: The ceffyl dŵr is said to inhabit mostly mountain pools and waterfalls, though it has been known to frequent rivers and seashores as well. It was believed to be a spirit assuming the shape of a horse, usually grey or black with a white mane, sometimes glowing or winged, to entice unwary travellers to ride him.

basis_claims.statement: The Dark Watchers is a group of entities in California folklore seen observing travelers along the Santa Lucia Mountains.
basis_claims.statement_id: Dark Watchers adalah kelompok entitas dalam cerita rakyat California yang mengamati pelancong di Pegunungan Santa Lucia.
basis_claims.quote: The Dark Watchers (also known by early Spanish settlers as Los Vigilantes Oscuros) is a name given to a group of entities in California folklore purportedly seen observing travelers along the Santa Lucia Mountains.

basis_claims.statement: The Dark Watchers are described as tall featureless dark silhouettes with brimmed hats or walking sticks.
basis_claims.statement_id: Dark Watchers digambarkan sebagai siluet hitam jangkung tanpa wajah yang mengenakan topi atau tongkat jalan.
basis_claims.quote: The Dark Watchers are described as tall, sometimes giant-sized featureless dark silhouettes often adorned with brimmed hats or walking sticks.

basis_claims.statement: They are most often reported to be seen in the hours around twilight and dawn.
basis_claims.statement_id: Mereka paling sering dilaporkan terlihat pada saat senja dan fajar.
basis_claims.quote: They are most often reported to be seen in the hours around twilight and dawn.

basis_claims.statement: Dragon of Mordiford, near Mordiford, Herefordshire, England; confluence of the River Lugg and River Wye.
basis_claims.statement_id: Naga Mordiford (Dragon of Mordiford), dekat desa Mordiford, Herefordshire, Inggris; pertemuan Sungai (River) Lugg dan Wye.
basis_claims.quote: The Dragon of Mordiford is a legendary creature that was said to reside just outside the Herefordshire village of Mordiford, at the confluence of the River Lugg and the River Wye.

basis_claims.statement: A wyvern found by the girl Maud in the forest; fed milk; winged.
basis_claims.statement_id: Wyvern ditemukan gadis Maud di hutan; diberi susu; bersayap.
basis_claims.quote: One version of the legend explains that the dragon – a wyvern in this account – was found by a little girl from Mordiford named Maud, who had desperately wanted a pet.

basis_claims.statement: The emerald dragon killed livestock and farmers; spared Maud.
basis_claims.statement_id: Naga hijau zamrud memangsa ternak dan petani; tak menyakiti Maud.
basis_claims.quote: Soon, it began to plague the local farms, killing their livestock, especially cows and sheep, and farmers were intolerant.

drangue.depicted_variant: Pogradec and Korca winged horse variant

basis_claims.statement: In the southeastern Albanian regions of Pogradec and Korça, the dragùa is envisaged as a beautiful strong winged horse defending civilisation and mankind.
basis_claims.statement_id: Di wilayah Pogradec dan Korça di Albania tenggara, dragùa dibayangkan sebagai kuda bersayap yang indah dan kuat yang membela peradaban dan umat manusia.
basis_claims.quote: In southeastern Albanian regions of Pogradec and Korça, the dragùa is "envisaged.. as a beautiful strong horse with wings, who defends civilization and mankind".

basis_claims.statement: In Philippine mythology, ekek (Ek Ek) are birdlike humans, winged beings who seek victims at night, hungry for flesh and blood, flying and manananggal-like but unable to split their bodies; unlike the wakwak, the ekek has a birdlike bill.
